name: No AI Only Grades
title: No AI Only Grades
answer: No AI Only Grades means every grade must be a teacher's decision. AI can help teachers grade faster, but it must never assign a grade that the teacher has not confirmed. This matters because grades affect students' futures, from course placement to college admission, and AI scoring may not match a school's own rubrics.

sections.body: The rule is that AI never issues a final grade. Teachers may use AI to grade faster, but the grade itself remains a human decision that the teacher confirms. The problem is that AI scoring does not think about student work the way teachers do, and its scores may not mean what they claim. Until a tool has been tested against a school's own rubrics, its output can only be a suggestion. This protects students from automated judgments that could affect their futures.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, teachers score the work themselves first and then use AI as a check, not as the first decision maker. A teacher can use Google Forms to collect short answers, have AI sort them into groups of similar responses, and then grade each group. The teacher still reads and scores every answer, but the process is faster. After a test, item analysis can show which questions many students missed, which guides reteaching. The text does not give grade band examples for this idea.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book cites a study of automated essay scoring with language models by Wang et al., 2026, which found that the tools weighted features of writing differently from the priorities in human rubrics, raising concerns about whether the scores meant what they claimed. It also notes that researchers have proposed frameworks to test the reliability and alignment of these tools (Liu et al., 2026). On the order of decisions, research has shown that when a machine decides first and a person is supposed to check, people rarely correct the machine's errors (Krugel et al., 2023). When the person decides first and the machine offers a second opinion, people keep their own judgment. The text does not give a separate evidence label for this idea.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The firm limit is that AI must never assign a grade the teacher has not confirmed. The risk is that AI scoring may not align with a school's rubrics, so its scores are suggestions at best until tested against those rubrics. Another risk is that if the machine decides first, people rarely correct its errors. The decision that stays with the teacher is the grade itself, and the teacher should score work first and use AI only as a check. Lower risk uses, such as sorting short answers or item analysis, still leave the teacher reading and scoring every answer.
